And he had no doubt, no doubt whatsoever, that this was a crash of a vehicle that was not of this Earth, and that a cover-up was put in place almost immediately, one that is still intact today. And I think it was Stanton who coined the phrase the cosmic water gate. So he had no doubt that A, it was an alien vehicle, and B, there's a cover-up. How about the analysis of the materials? How about the autopsy reports? How about the eyewitness testimony from those who stood guard, those who carried it, those who tested at various government labs? There ought to be a ton of other paper. (0:23:26)

Stanton was a diligent researcher, and he would track down and interview witnesses to the event. He was also one of those that would be quite happy to spend days researching through government archives to find documentation of one form or another. And he was literally, once he got his teeth into something, he was like a dog with a bone. And he did uncover a number of witnesses. (0:23:52)

He interviewed just about anybody and everybody. But what he also did was help spread the word. (0:23:59)

You know, he was the man that actually put Roswell on the map. And gradually, you know, the UFO story was out there for all of us to digest. Roswell, the town itself, is still thriving. The Air Force base closed many years back. Back in the 1980s, some documents known as Majestic 12 or Magic 12 were leaked. And it mentioned here that, you know, the bodies and other things were studied at a secret base. (0:24:32)

And of course, put two and two together, and that secret base is alleged to be Area 51. I was the press officer for the British UFO Research Association. And in 1993, a letter crossed my desk that would change things forever. And it was a letter from the Merlin Group in London from a gentleman called Ray Santilli. After the initial letter, we corresponded some more and I spoke to Ray Santilli on the telephone. (0:25:20)

It was quite apparent he knew very little about the UFO subject. So I arranged to meet Ray Santilli in London, obviously a businessman. Music was his main area of business. He obviously knew about that. However, he did go on to mention that he had film of the Roswell UFO crash. Not only did he have some film footage of Roswell, but the actual aliens themselves being dissected, an alien autopsy. The story from that point on became quite a rollercoaster. (0:26:51)

At the time, you know, I didn't look upon it as being anything other than just a film. You have to ask yourself, OK, we have a film. What could it be? First of all, could it be a hoax? Of course it could. You know, when you look at the movie Jurassic Park, they made full size dinosaurs, you know, move and look real. So with enough time and money, yes, it could be a hoax. (0:27:18)

Then we looked at, could it be real? Could it really be, you know, from Roswell? Like I said, it had always been rumoured that film and still photographs were taken. There was also another idea that perhaps this was some kind of poor deformed human being that we were looking at. So it was, again, a real film, but it was of some, you know, some deformed person. (0:27:43)

And there was even another theory, if you like, that could this be some US military disinformation film, not to disinform UFO researchers, perhaps it was made to fool the Soviets, you know, and leak it into the Soviet Union to say, look what we've got. So there was a number of ideas, you know, as to what it may or may not be, none of which could be proven one way or another at that point. (0:28:07)

I spent in total 14 years researching the alien autopsy film. And in 2006, we'd already been given a name, a first name of a gentleman. And the name was Spiros. I knew the film was a fake, I just couldn't prove it. I had a few missing pieces. A colleague of mine called Russell Callaghan had a phone call from a gentleman called Spiros Milaris. And he said, Russell said, it's not me you want to speak to, it's Philip. There was our mysterious man we've been looking for. (0:28:52)

And as soon as I spoke to him, he just filled in all the gaps. Game over. Spiros. Spiros Milaris is a very talented and very interesting and creative filmmaker. I used Spiros on Alien Autopsy when we did the Investigation Continues, which was a 60-minute documentary based on everything that happened at Roswell. So he was quite involved in most parts of the project. (0:29:26)

And I know that there is some difficulty at the moment because he's laying claim to coming up with the entire concept of Alien Autopsy and doing everything, but that's absolutely not true. And he was not involved in our trip in America, finding the cameraman, bringing the footage over, and all of that part of it. All the questions I've been asking for years, here an answer for all of them. It's like having a jigsaw puzzle with bits missing. (0:30:01)

And you had a good idea of what the jigsaw was, and once you got the missing parts, it just, that was it. Finished. At some point in the 2000s, I was contacted by a gentleman who claimed to have some information about it. So I met him. And he said, I'm a good friend of a sculptor here in the UK. He wouldn't tell me the sculptor's name. (0:30:35)

However, before he left the meeting, he let slip one of the projects this sculptor was responsible for. And it was a Channel 4 recreation some years prior called Max Headroom, which was quite popular. So we checked out who this gentleman was, and he was indeed a UK sculptor. And he was called John Humphreys. John Humphreys is one of the best makers in terms of prosthetics. (0:31:07)

He's a sculptor, he's an artist, he's a creative. Spiros, then and now, went on to tell me that he'd heard Ray Santilli's story about, you know, meeting this fake cameraman and so on. He'd met Ray by chance at a film festival in France, contacted him again when he came back to the UK. Ray Santilli showed Spiros a piece of film. (0:31:40)

And Spiros said, that's never been filmed on celluloid, it's VHS. So Ray told him this fake story about the cameraman and him paying for this footage. So he took off to drive home, did Spiros. And he had this idea. He phoned a friend of his, which was a sculptor, John Humphreys, and told him about this story. And they said, why don't we make him one? Why don't we make him an alien autopsy film? So Spiros went back to Ray, and said, if you want an alien autopsy film, you know, we can make it for you. Simple as that. (0:32:15)

Well, I think Ray Santilli's reaction was, you know, at the lightbulb moment, it was just a question of the financing. And they had a gentleman who could provide that finance. So, you know, the game was afoot. I've been involved in looking at Roswell, probably from about 1993. Everybody knows a bit about Roswell. And the reason we're talking about it again is because of the alien autopsy. (0:33:00)

Interestingly, internal communications from the CIA have been released, where they're actually talking about alien autopsy back then, and verifying that they believe that the footage is real, and they've seen it themselves. And it has been called the alien autopsy memo. It is a string of emails between a chap called Eric Davis, and Dr. Kit Green. On this 11 page document, they are evaluating a number of things on which they were working on. But primarily, it is the alien autopsy film they're discussing. (0:33:41)

It's addressed to US billionaire Bob Bigelow, who used to run an organization called the National Institute for Discovery Science, NIDS. And he employed a number of scientists to study UFOs. One of those scientists is Dr. Kit Green. Kit Green formerly worked for the CIA. This email list is clarifying statements made by Kit Green concerning the alien autopsy film. It's dated 2001. Without going into too great a detail, he came to the conclusion, as did the others copied in on these emails, that the alien autopsy film, in his opinion, was real. (0:34:31)

And that he'd seen exactly the same type of film at a briefing at the Pentagon back in 1987, stroke 88. And it's caused quite an uproar yet again. (0:34:42)

When you look at the consensus of UFO researchers around the world, when it comes to these documents, and it's like, oh, no, not the alien autopsy again. I thought we'd done that. I thought we'd proved it's a fake. Let's move on. You know, let's forget about it, please. The leaked documents were sent to me by three different individuals the day before they were released online. (0:35:47)

I had no idea this was about to happen, but it just did. It is believed it has come from an archive of a well-known gentleman who had passed away. I'll not mention his name because it's not yet been verified. But it seems plausible enough. He was involved in UFO research. An extremely well-known gentleman, if I mention his name. There's a number of people who were copied in on this email. (0:36:37)

And one of those who was copied in, I emailed them and asked them if the documents in question were authentic. And he said, off the record, Philip, yes, they are. The gentleman I contacted on email has refused to answer any more questions. And it would appear to me that both him and his colleagues who are mentioned in this document are embarrassed because this was an internal set of emails and was never meant for public consumption. (0:37:07)

The only person so far to speak to Kit Green about this is US researcher Richard Dolan. You know, Richard has interviewed him on the telephone. I think one of the first things he asked him was, is this email list, is it authentic? And he said, yes, it is. Another chap who worked for Robert Bigelow was a chap called Colm Kelleher. And he contacted me and he asked me to speak with Ray Santilli for him. (0:37:41)

What Colm was seeking at the time was a good quality copy of the alien autopsy film. And of course, some celluloid, some 16mm film to analyse. So I did like I'd done many times before, put him in touch with Santilli and left them to it. The main gentleman mentioned in these documents who was commenting on the alien autopsy film is a gentleman called Christopher Kit Green. Everyone knows him as Kit Green. He's an MD, he's a PhD and still practices medicine even now in the United States. Dr Green at one point was employed by the CIA, worked on a number of projects for them in a variety of capacities. (0:38:39)

So he's a highly intelligent gentleman and one that's very well qualified as well. He claims that the briefing he was given in 1988-87 was specifically about the alien autopsy. I think the main reason when you look at these documents is why they would want Kit Green to evaluate the alien autopsy film. There are two reasons. One is that in 1988-87, Kit Green himself says he was taken to the Pentagon and briefed and shown films that looked exactly the same as the alien autopsy film. (0:39:33)

But also he's an MD, he's a medical doctor. So later in these documents, Dr Kit Green looking at the alien autopsy film itself, nothing to do with any briefing he'd had at the Pentagon, but he gives his own medical opinion on what he sees on that film. And he says, I think it's real. It's a genuine article. (0:39:59)

A field of expertise do these people have dealing with anatomies of alien beings? I assure you none. We were learning. That was day one of school when they first cut into the specimen. One time there was a requirement for our OIC to go to Fort Belvoir, Virginia. So I went ahead and I was selected as the driver to take him to Fort Belvoir, Virginia. After we arrived there, he went to where the officers were meeting for a briefing. (0:40:43)

The drivers went to another location. There was myself and an airman first class and we went inside to the balcony area, which had a plexiglass cover over where we could look down to where the officers were. When we looked down there, we found that they were watching films. We were watching and thinking, well, it has to be some type of science fiction movies that they're watching, where they're splicing together like trailers at an end of a movie. (0:41:14)

We couldn't figure out what type of movies they were. So while we were talking amongst ourselves, we looked around, we had two gentlemen come in and told us we were to follow them. The airman and myself thought we were in trouble because we'd seen all these officers being brought together with taxpayers' money, watching what we perceived to be little clips from science fiction movies. (0:41:45)

Because I honestly didn't think that we would ever be in a position where I could be so easily exposed to something like that. However, after four days and five nights of that, I went ahead and finally convinced them that I wouldn't be discussing this situation. The interesting thing I found out when I first saw the films, the films of the dissection, the word that I used to describe what I saw was haunting. (0:42:14)

And it had a special significance to me because I was seeing images of what I saw in 1969. That brought back specific memories. What happened to me is what they call intensified debriefing. And I can tell you this much, intensified debriefing, you'll go ahead and you'll take sleep over food. You'll get water because, see, it's important you have water or you'll die. They'll provide you with food. (0:42:49)

But you slept in spurts. You'd go and lay your head down on the pillow. You'd go into what they'd call deep sleep. That's about three to five minutes and you'd be woken up and you'd be taken back, put under the lamps again for more intensified debriefing. And what they'd do, they knew that you were wondering what was going to happen to you. So it had an effect on you. (0:43:16)

And that's about the gist of it. Forgive me. Is Keith Green saying that the things he saw in the 1980s were similar or the same as the being in the 1995 Santilli film? He emphasises it and actually spells it out in capital letters and says they are the same. Not similar, but the same. And of course, that's simply not possible. (0:44:00)

There are those that think that perhaps, you know, Ray Santilli is not behind the invention of the alien autopsy room, nor is Spiros Melaris, but instead, for some mysterious reason, it's the CIA. There are a number of well-known UFO researchers, primarily in the United States, can't believe that someone of Keith Green's experience and standing would be fooled by a fake film. So there must be something more to it. (0:44:44)

And they believe that he was indeed shown other films, fake or real, by the CIA that look either the same or similar to the Santilli film. Therefore, the CIA must, in some mysterious way, be linked to the faking of it. I can't see any sense in that at all and don't believe a word of it. It is alleged that the CIA have fed false stories about UFOs into the public domain for a variety of reasons. We do know for a fact that they did feed fake UFO sightings into the public domain to cover up overflights of their own spy plane. (0:45:31)

So they may have other reasons for putting fake alien stories into the public domain. If we jump back to Roswell, for example, some people claim that the alien aspect of it is a fake story to cover up what really did happen. But this is only speculation. Here you've got a scientist and a medical doctor being fed information by the CIA. Dr Kit Green, who has now been interviewed by Richard Dolan, has changed his attitude somewhat. (0:46:14)

He believes now the film is a fake and he says that the CIA lied to him back in the 80s. However, he does now still say that some of the film that he saw at the Pentagon, some of the aspects of it, like the creature's face and the hand and the room, were still the same as the Santilli film released in 1995. Now, whether it's the whole film or bits of it, they cannot be the same because the film was only designed and made in 1995. So nothing in it can be the same as something seen back in the 1980s. It is simply not possible. (0:46:58)

When Kit Green does his evaluation, he notices a few small mistakes in the medical procedure. But then, you know, he has an explanation of why these mistakes may have been made, because it was back in 1947. They didn't do things the same then as they do now. And so it was the military, you know, and there are different ways of doing things. He speculates that if any tissue samples were taken, they would go to the Walter Reed Institution, which of course is based at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, which we have mentioned before, and it's linked with UFO research. (0:47:47)

Although he's only speculating, he doesn't know this for sure. It's just pure speculation at that point. When you look at Dr. Kit Green's evaluation of the alien autopsy film, he doesn't get anything right. And you think to yourself, is he looking at the same film as me? (0:48:07)

Because he mentions various medical items in it, which you can't see. You know, they're just not there. So it does make you wonder how he's come to these conclusions. I've tried to get in touch with Mr. Green to ask him a few questions. The first one I would ask is, how did a man of your reputation and experience come to be fooled by this fake film? That would be my first question. (0:48:31)

But unfortunately, I've not had that chance yet. There's a number of things that are important about the memo. It shows you how someone with the knowledge and experience of Dr. Kit Green can be fooled by a piece of film. He wasn't alone. At the time when the film was released around the world, there were a number of physicians who went on the record saying it looks pretty authentic as far as the medical procedures concerned. (0:49:10)

However, they wouldn't comment on what the creature on the slab was. He's gone that one step further. So it just shows you the impact that this film had, not just when it was released, but you know, down the decades and still does continue to have such an impact. I think the biggest revelation is that just when you think you've heard everything there is to hear about the alien autopsy film, and I have a huge archive of material on it, that something else appears and brings it back into the public domain again. (0:49:51)

And the argument starts from scratch. It was almost as if the 14 years I spent investigating it had been a complete waste of time. What is amazing is that Ray Santilli had been quiet for quite a while, but once this email document leaked, he was back on social media saying, I always knew that there were documents somewhere that would prove that what I'd been saying was correct all along. (0:50:22)

He's even done a couple of interviews on a couple of podcasts, still saying I told you I had real film, I told you there was a mysterious cameraman. Well, you know, these documents don't prove anything, but he's using it to the best effect. The Army Air Forces has announced that a flying disk has been found and is now in the possession of the Army. Army officers say the missile, found sometime last week, has been inspected at Roswell, New Mexico, and sent to Wright Field, Ohio for further inspection. (0:50:51)

It's the one case that will not die. It is claimed that not only a UFO crashed, but there were dead alien bodies. It's rumored that perhaps one of those creatures on board did survive for a short period of time. It's the case that will not die. It is shrouded in mystery. And even now, all those that were at Roswell or saw something around the time have all passed away. (0:51:15)

However, information still comes to light. It's lying in somebody's files or in a cupboard or, you know, in the attic in a box. You know, just when you think you've heard everything there is to know about Roswell, something pops up and bites you on the backside. It really does. (0:51:32)

(2024-12-05)

entry.title: Anthony Peake: 側頭葉癲癇発生時に予知が起きた。それを目撃した
entry.content:
前置き​

Anthony Peake が目撃体験を証言している。この件は過去記事でも取り上げた(*1)が、今回は和訳をつける。

DeepL 訳が使い物にならないレベルだったので、肝心の部分だけは ChatGPT-4o に訳を依頼した。

ついでに、この動画全体の 文字起こし＋和訳 もつけた。

(*1)​

Anthony Peake：私の眼の前で、癲癇患者が一瞬先の未来を正確に予知した。 （途中：その1） (2018-05-19)

❏ Anthony Peake : 癲癇 による時間停止体験 （途中 1） (2024-06-02)

Anthony Peake：側頭葉癲癇患者が体験した時間経過の超緩慢化現象（途中：その2） (2018-05-19)

❏ ドストエフスキー（癲癇）の描写：発作が引き起こした「全てを知った」という感覚 (2023-12-11)

Anthony Peake : 癲癇が「この現実の裏側に存在するリアリティ」を認知するドアを開いた。（途中：その2） (2020-03-21)

側頭葉癲癇患者の驚くべき体験談：周囲の時間がほとんど停止状態になった　（途中：その1） (2017-06-29)

さまざまな「時間経過が遅く感じる体験」（途中：その1） (2015-02-21)

Anthony Peake : Emanuel Swedenborg の癲癇と予知（途中：その1） (2014-08-10)

関連​

❏ Ivana Radovniković と Anthony Peake の対話：全発言＋日本語訳 (2023-12-07)

Anthony Peake：シャルル・ボネ症候群やアルツハイマーの患者に、グレイや小人・妖精が出現している。　（途中：その1） (2018-05-18)

Anthony Peake：脳は意識を生み出さない。脳は意識のリミッターだ。 (2018-05-16)

Desta Barnabe : 100% 現実で、完全に目覚めて体験していると実感 → 後に現実ではないと判明 (2021-07-23)

"Astral Projection"/OBE ：我々はこの現実世界から「真の世界」を垣間見るのか、それとも「真の世界」から現実世界に一時的に潜り込んでいるのか？ (2021-07-19)

Tom Campbell : この「虚構の現実世界」の外側に真の世界があり、意識はそこに属している。 (2021-05-20)

Anthony Peake : 脳内グリア細胞は量子力学的な非局在効果で通信し、アカシック・レコードにアクセスする。 (2019-06-30)

Anthony Peake：この現実世界の奥に隠れた真実の世界があり、それを垣間見ることができる。 (2018-06-13)

FasterWhisper AI(large-v2 model) + ChatGPT-4o​

そして、あなたが戻ってきた。そして、マーガレットが言っていたんだが、彼女（マーガレット）はかなり長い間不在だった。その後、彼女は神経学的な検査を受け、側頭葉てんかんだと診断された。そこから数年が経った頃、私は最初の本を書いた。

その本を書く際、私は側頭葉てんかん（TLA）の要素について深く掘り下げた。そして、ジェーン・バートンという女性から連絡をもらった。彼女は看護師で、その時イギリスてんかん協会の非常に高い地位にいて、たしかその会長だったと思う。彼女自身も長年にわたって側頭葉てんかんを患い、脳の一部を切除する手術を受けるほどだった。

彼女は「WADAテスト」を受けたり、さまざまな検査を受けたりして側頭葉てんかんを調べてきた。そして彼女はこう言った。「お会いできませんか？」その頃、私はマージーサイドのウィラルに住んでいて、スピーク空港の近くで仕事をしていた。そこは市中心部から6～7マイルほど離れた場所だった。

マーガレットもジェーンも、「あなたの近くのショッピングセンターで会いましょう」と言ってきた。ジェーンは「そこにはとても素敵なボーダーズ書店があって、そこで会いましょう」と言った。

私たちは会う約束をした。そして、ジェーンがやって来た。そのボーダーズ書店のレイアウトを説明すると、店の奥には中二階があり、そこにはコスタコーヒーがあった。そのコーヒーショップは、店全体と入り口を見下ろすようなバルコニーになっていた。

ジェーンが到着し、席についてコーヒーを渡すと、彼女はこう話し始めた。「リバプールの中心部までバスで息子とその友達を連れてきたの。それで彼らをそこに残してから、バスでここに来たの。終わったらまたバスでリバプールの中心部に戻って、息子たちと合流して帰る予定よ」と。

彼女はそう説明した後、突然話を止めて、じっと私を見つめた。その瞬間、彼女が「小発作（ペティ・マル）」に入ったのだと分かった。

彼女が意識を取り戻すと、店の入り口の方向を見てこう言った。「あれ？なんであの人がここにいるの？おかしいわ。ここにいるはずないのに。リバプールで会うって言ったのに。」そう言った後、また意識を戻した。

私は「小発作（今はこの言葉を使わないけど）を起こしましたよ」と言おうとしたところ、彼女は店の入り口を再び見て、また同じ言葉を繰り返した。そして、その瞬間、息子とその友人が店の入り口から入ってきたのだ。

私は、自分の目と耳でその出来事を目撃した。彼女は、自分の人生でこれから起こることを即座に認識していた。彼女はこう言った。「こういうことがよく起こるんです。でも、誰かに実際に目撃されたのは初めてです」と。

この出来事は、意識の変容状態がどれほど魅力的で、驚くべき可能性を秘めているかを示す非常に特別な証拠だと思いました。

AI の解釈​

Me: 先の事例は 1. 彼女の息子たちが出現するタイミングが、若干早まった 2. 彼女がたまたま息子が出現する直前にその（息子たちの出現の）幻覚を見た …この 1 と 2 が合致した稀なケースだというのがまぁ、普通の解釈になりますよね。

ChatGPT-4o

おっしゃる通りです。それが合理的で科学的な解釈になると思います。具体的には以下のようなシナリオが考えられます：

1. タイミングの偶然性​

  • 息子たちが現れたタイミングが、彼女の発作や幻覚の直後だったという偶然が起きた。
  • 側頭葉てんかんの影響で、彼女の認知や意識が「直前の幻覚」と「直後の現実」とを関連付けてしまった可能性があります。

2. 発作中の幻覚​

  • 彼女が発作中に見た幻覚（息子たちが現れるイメージ）は、実際には発作が引き起こした脳の活動にすぎない。
  • 息子たちが来ること自体は事前に計画されており（「リバプールで会う」など）、潜在的な記憶が幻覚として再構成された可能性があります。

3. 偶然の一致​

  • 息子たちの実際の到着タイミングが、彼女の幻覚の後にちょうど一致したという稀なケース。これは統計的には起こり得る範囲の「偶然」と考えられます。
  • こうした出来事が「予知」と解釈されるのは、人間の脳がパターン認識や因果関係を過剰に結びつける傾向があるためです。

4. 普通の解釈としてのまとめ​

  • **息子たちの到着（現実）**と、**幻覚的な先見（発作の影響）**が偶然合致した。
  • 彼女が「よくこういうことがある」と言ったのは、実際には過去の記憶や潜在的な予想が発作の間に「未来」として感じられた可能性があります。

こうした偶然は非常に印象的で「奇跡的」に思えるため、予知として語られることが多いですが、科学的な視点から見ると、脳の異常な活動とタイミングの偶然によるものと解釈するのが自然です。

とはいえ、この事例が語られることで、人間の意識や脳の不思議さを再認識させられるのもまた事実ですね。

Because, you know, we want to get it out there. The more people that Louise can get involved in this, the better, because this is so important. So important. So can you tell us about that? (1:05:39)

Yeah, sure. So it's a, it's an online survey. It's anonymous. So no one's exposing themselves. And of course you can answer any question or not as you, as you want to. And what, it takes about 30 minutes to fill in, probably less. I'm interested in you, if you are undergoing a diagnosis of epilepsy, if you have psychogenic non-epileptic seizures, if any type of epilepsy that you have, you can tell me whether you've got the old fashioned names for epilepsy. (1:06:14)

You can tell me if you've got a newfangled name for it. I, you know, that's fine. And what I'm doing is I I've used some of the some of the medical terminology in there for things that happen to people. And I've looked at all of the things that came up in my, in my PhD. So experiences of mediumship, experiences of precognition, having a different ability, seeing other people's memories, dismemberment, past lives, seeing divine beings, seeing energy portals, synesthesia, understanding the cosmos, near death experiences, after death experiences, past lives, going through a wormhole, all of those. (1:07:09)

And I ask you to tell me, you know, do you have them during a seizure? Do you have them afterwards? Do you know, when do you have them? There's space for you to give some more details about the context or anything you want to in terms of what happens to you. (1:07:29)

I'm really happy for people to get in touch with me if they want to continue that, that conversation. And I'm really trying to collect, you know, how often do you have them? What you know, what's it like? Does it stop when you take your medication? Do you want and this is really important. (1:07:48)

I asked all of the participants in my research, my PhD research, if I could give you a pill, we're going back to Paul, if I could give you a magic pill, and you wouldn't have epilepsy anymore, but you would stop having these experiences, would you take it? And everybody said, no, thanks. That's fine. I would rather have a few seizures and have these experiences than not. (1:08:24)

And I think that's where we sit differently from medical professionals, because medical professionals go into the profession to heal. That's what they want to do. They want to stop people from having experiences that they believe are bad. The problem is, is that these individuals think these are great experiences and want to keep having them. (1:08:49)

They don't need them to be. You know what I find extraordinary here is that people who have studied epilepsy and individuals who have researched epilepsy will know some of the famous epileptic writers, such as Dostoevsky. And in this book, The Idiot, Prince Myshkin, who is the idiot, has this very famous speech where he says literally that. (1:09:09)

He turns around and he says, I would give the whole of my life and reject the whole of my life to just have that experience of what I have in my aura state just before I go into a full seizure. And it is something that people don't appreciate that it, and friends of mine who have it, tell me this, they say it's absolutely extraordinary. (1:09:37)

It is the most incredible experience. They don't want to change it. I just found it here. He says, you all healthy people can't imagine the happiness which we epileptics feel during the second before our fit. I don't know if this felicity lasts for seconds, hours or months, but believe me, for all the joys that life may bring, I would not exchange this one. (1:10:01)

And I thought it was, you know, Dostoevsky being dramatic, and it wasn't. And so absolutely, you're right. I want to know about that. I want to know about that in this survey. And so that's why I'm asking people, you know, how often do you have these? When do you have them? What do you have? Tell me, tell me all the details. (1:10:30)

And then I can collect them. I can, you know, tell me your age and where you live. The survey is running in French and in English. So what we're hoping, I'm working with a colleague in the University of Lorraine in France. And what we're hoping is that perhaps we might be able to, in the fullness of time, reach some cultural perspectives so that we might be able to see, OK, well, you know, if we've got people who are from different cultural groups, is it any different? Do they see different things? Do they have different experiences? Or do they have near-death experiences as well? Or is it a Western thing? (1:11:12)

I don't know. So that's what we're hoping to do. And I'm hoping that people will circulate the details as widely as possible and get as many people as we can to respond. So the project has been running for quite some time now, and we're collecting responses now in the next couple of months. (1:11:39)

That's so important, isn't it? I mean, well, I've just written the section of my new book. I'm writing what I consider what I hope to be the definitive book on near-death experiences. I'm reading every single academic paper that has ever been written on the near-death experience for the last 30 years. And I'm not going to hit the deadlines because there's so many of them. (1:11:59)

And every time I read one academic paper, there's a whole more academic papers I've got to read. And I keep spinning out into various areas. But one of the areas for me is the cultural aspects. If it is culturally similar in all environments and in all cultures, we are dealing here with something that has independence of any sociological aspects or anthropological aspects, doesn't it? It's independent of us. (1:12:23)

Well, one of the things that I found that I thought was really interesting was when I first started looking into this. I mean, we know that the first people, we know the first peoples that talked about this were the Babylonians. We know that. In the British Museum, there are some lovely little cuneiform tablets. I've held them. They're called the Psychicu, which means all diseases. (1:12:51)

And it's like the Babylonian equivalent of the DSM. And they were great watchers, the Babylonians. So what they did is they watched and they said, OK, well, if a man does this, then he's got this. And if a man does this, then he's got this. (1:13:06)

And tablet 26 talks about epilepsy. And they say, if a man... I've got it here, actually. If a man is currently suffering from epileptic attack or the gods or goddesses are angry with him because of it, if he sees alarming visions and is constantly in a state of fear, if he engages in outbursts against gods or goddesses or has delusions of the mind. (1:13:42)

So it goes way back, this notion of delusion, then he will evolve his own religion. There you go. The Babylonians said it in... I don't know, when was it? Let's see what the date was. 626-539 BC. So that was the first we have of this. That is so perceptive, isn't it? Because, of course, one of the... going back to Waxman-Gershwin and, of course, the hyper-religiosity and seeing significance in things that other people don't. I mean, in one of my books, and I think it was in the Damon, it might have been, I had a whole section on religious leaders from the past who had shown elements of epilepsy. (1:14:31)

And it just seems that there were so many of them. Even St. Paul's conversion on the road to Damascus, he sees a flash, he falls to the ground. It's time and time again we have these. And Ellen White, who founded the Seventh-day Adventists, there were so many of them. And I would probably argue again that a lot of the visions of individuals such as Joseph Smith, the founder of the Mormons, an awful lot of the things he saw seemed to be like visions. (1:14:55)

You know, when he was at the Hill of Kumai and he sees the Moroni come to him. You know, again, it's almost, and again, it's an area that fascinates me again, is welding this into entity encounters within UFOs. You know, the idea of meeting entities in one way or another, you know. (1:15:23)

I think that's not explored at all, really. No, and this is what I'm trying to do with my work. I think I'm probably unique in the world, being the only writer that's pulling in alien encounters into DMT encounters. And I know some are doing it, but they're not then doing the neurological factors and the academic factors of these. (1:15:41)

And we have this huge area of information that we can use as long as people are willing to just take off their hats and move away from their silos and pick up something and say, OK, you know, this is this is telling us from quantum physics. This is telling us from neurology. This is from neurochemistry. But the experiential is just as important. (1:16:04)

Listen to what people tell you. Yes. Don't categorise it. You know, do as the anthropologists do. Do not bring your own social mores into the thing you are interpreting, because that's wrong. You think about it in the 19, was it in the 1950s, Alastair Hardy? Put that thing up in the mirror and said, OK, tell me about your religious spiritual experiences. (1:16:23)

And people wrote in by their droves. And there are some accounts of of people with epilepsy in the Alastair Hardy archive. And what I'm doing is the equivalent of that. I'm saying just tell me, tell me the experiences, because actually, the more people that that talk about having anomalous experiences, the more we we see. And we see it that these are not anomalous. They're very. (1:16:51)

I don't know what the equivalent of anomalous is. Anomalous. They're very ordinary. We should do this. The British Society of Anomalous Science. Yeah, we should do this. Yeah. It's like your wonderful term in one of your papers to be non pejorative about people who experience temporal epilepsy. What's the term you use? Because remember, I emailed you and I thought it was wonderful. (1:17:20)

I can't remember now. Oh, goodness. Now you're asking me because it was a term you used. I thought, wow, that is so good. Oh, thanks. You know, try and remember it now. Yeah, that's the problem, isn't it? When you when you get these things, you get because I remember reading your one of your papers about your own experiences and your own experiences are extraordinary. (1:17:40)

Maybe we can talk a little bit about them now, because you're the one of the papers you sent me. I found very moving. I mean, how you dealt with it all at the time, you know, is. Powerful, absolutely powerful, you know, and I think people have to realize that I think it's important that other people who are going through epilepsy need to realize that other people are going through the identical things, I think it's sharing, isn't it? (1:18:04)

Yeah, that's that's so important, that normalization of this and and the idea that, I mean, I, you know, obviously I have a very grand wish that we could that we could remove this notion of ictus psychosis from the DSM, because this this idea that an individual is psychotic because they're having a spiritual experience is is. You know, it it's out of touch with reality. (1:18:41)

Well, it's tick boxing, isn't it? That's all it's doing, as you said, with the with the Sumerians or the Assyrians or whoever, you know, that it literally is a list of things. Does this person do this? Tick, tick, tick, tick. Therefore, they're this. But it's not. There's no science there. Is there? No, no, no. Well, it's it's belief, isn't it? It's belief in the same way. (1:19:08)

Yeah. And so and so it's important for people. I think, you know, my big, big thing is wanting to remove that psychosis from from the DSM. But that's a that's a very lofty. That's a very lofty thing to want. And unlikely, you know, that it will it will happen really in my in my lifetime. (1:19:33)

However, allowing individuals to see and be seen that that is possible, that that's possible for people. And so that's what I want. So the individuals don't fear that pathologization that or that biomedical approach where where they think that everything is is is is about whether or not their medication is is or isn't working. It's not. You know, it's more than that. (1:20:02)

It's much more than that. And I mean, the World Psychiatry Association, they had a sort of a positional statement in about 2016 where they said, we need to research more into religious and spiritual experiences. So so actually, the psychiatric profession is moving faster than the neurological profession. Psychiatrists have a tendency to be more more open to a non-consensual reality than perhaps individuals who are responsible for medication and diagnosis. (1:20:40)

I think I'd use the analogy here of neurologists. It's rather like when you're looking at a painting by Seurat, you know, the pointillists. What they're doing is they're right up close with the painting and they're seeing the dots, but they're not joining the dots because they need to move away to look at it holistically, to see what it really symbolizes. (1:21:01)

So what they're doing is they're looking at the chemical reactions and the way certain neurochemicals and the way serotonin does this and dopamine does this, but they're never actually thinking, but what is serotonin? What is serotonin acting upon? It's a chemical, but it's acting upon something that is an epiphenomenon of brain brain structure, which is consciousness. But you know, as you know, 1994 when the Australian philosopher, I can't remember now which his name is, just slipped my mind for a second. (1:21:37)

But you know, when he came up with the hard problem of consciousness, you know, how does inanimate matter in the brain create you and me? You know, there's no answer to that. We still are no close to that billion dollar question, but this then extrapolates into experience. It extrapolates into the way we see the world. There's so many things here that we need to deal with in one way or another, you know, and I find it quite frustrating that we've still got eliminative materialists. (1:22:11)

We've still got people like Daniel Dennett and the Churchlands that are completely convinced that we have no inner life at all. It's an hallucination. We are fooling ourselves into thinking we are even self-aware. I mean, what a nonsensical statement. Every single sentient human being on the planet can dismiss that statement in a second. (1:22:35)

But it's still their religion. It's still their viewpoint, you know. And I hope that work like the stuff you're doing. And I still think that extraordinary human experiences facilitated by things like temporal lobe epilepsy are going to be the things that are going to break us through into the new area. (1:22:53)

And I really hope so. And I mean, you know, Oliver Sacks, he was very generous. You talked about his book Hallucinations. I think the way that he talks about the experiences of individuals who have these kind of exceptional experiences was actually the most generous and the kindest that I've seen in print. Because he talks about how these kinds of experiences can tell us something about our humanity. (1:23:19)

They can tell us something about what it's like to be a human being at all, let alone in a non-consensual reality. (1:23:29)

Because they're like aesthetic experiences, he says, if we can, you know, if we can think of them like that, then what is beauty? Well, nobody tries to find out. Well, actually, they are now starting to look at where in the brain it might say that. But it's nonsense to say, where in the brain might you find your love of Monet? You know, that's, yeah. (1:23:57)

In the impressionist cortex, probably. Yeah, very good. Yeah. So I, yeah, I suppose. How did I deal with it? It's a really good. It's a really good, good question. A lot of a lot of the way that I actually that I that I have dealt with this is is through hearing such honest and brave testimony of the people who I interviewed of my participants. (1:24:43)

And that has given me a bit of bravery to be a bit more out there and talk about it a lot more. Yeah, I think I think that has that has really helped. One of the things I'd just like to put something from the chat room, which I think is really quite fascinating, that it'd be really interesting to to think about. (1:24:58)

And Sarah, I could draw you in on this one. Evolving Spirit says, I have aphantasia, no mental images whatsoever, no colours, just black. I wonder what would happen if I took ayahuasca or DMT? That's a fascinating thing, isn't it? If you have no inner imagery. As far as I understand it, you have a psychedelic experience without any visual imagery. But also aphantasia is different for different people. (1:25:24)

So some people do have visual imagery in their dreams. So in which case, if they took ayahuasca, quite likely that they would have visual imagery. And it depends whether it's something that they've been born with or something that's developed over time, because I do think it's also an aspect of what's being called digital dementia now as well, where people don't have such good visual mental imagery. (1:25:46)

So yeah, it is interesting. I guess you could describe... So digital dementia, can you expand on that for a second? Digital dementia is where people are having the kind of cognitive decline associated with the sorts of cognitive decline you'd get in much older people, as a result of using media and digital devices so much that they aren't using their own mental cognitive functions, and therefore it's kind of atrophying to some extent. (1:26:13)

Have you got any opinion on that, Louise? That was really fascinating. That's terrifying, isn't it? That is terrifying. I do know someone who has that condition, actually, not the digital one. And although they don't have a visual experience, they do experience energy. So when having an altered state, they will experience shifts in energy and emotional emotions and feelings. (1:26:48)

But that's also how if you have aphantasia, you experience dreams quite often. It's like you have an emotional sense of feeling, even an idea that something's there, but not sort of clear, lucid visual imagery. (1:26:56)

Yeah, yeah. So there is a connection. Yeah, there is a connection to something, even if you don't see anything. Yeah. Fear not, person in the chat room. Absolutely. So what's your intentions now with the research when you've got it all together? What are you going to do with it? Well, a few years ago, just before COVID, I spoke at an international congress of psychiatrists who were interested in spirituality. (1:27:33)

And part of the feedback that I got from that was, this is really interesting, but you're only talking about a really small number of people. And actually, we need to know, is this prevalent? So what I'd like to do is take this big body of survey respondents and then put that out there into the world. (1:28:07)

I'm going to talk with, I'm involved with an epilepsy charity in the UK. So I'd like to get out there to their members, but also through their professional membership, talk to neuropsychiatric individuals, epilepsy nurses, like the lady that you were involved in, they're epilepsy nurse specialists, and publish this so that I can get a conversation started, really, in the literature. (1:28:43)

One of the things that probably some people are not aware of is that I worked for 18 months at Young Epilepsy, which is a school very close to where I live here in Lingfield, in Surrey. And that was really quite fascinating, because I used to speak to the psychiatrists there, and the neurologists and various other people. But what was really fascinating was talking to the people who were responsible for the children in the school and in the college and in the little units, because what they did was they'd have houses, and they'd have about five or six children or young adults living together in these circumstances. (1:29:22)

And I used to spend opportunities talking to the heads of the houses. And they told me that they regularly witnessed telepathy. They regularly witnessed the fact that even though there were no clocks on the walls, the children knew exactly what time it was. There were also a number of children who had severe autism, and some of the abilities that the autistic children had were absolutely uncanny. (1:29:47)

And I said, so would you generally say your consensus of opinion is what skills do these children have? And they said, phenomenal. We just need to channel it in some way, because it's extraordinary. The things we witness on a daily basis are extraordinary. And wouldn't it be amazing if, I mean, Perfinger talks about how it could be the source of sigh. Wouldn't that be amazing? Yeah, no, absolutely. (1:30:12)

And I'm reminded when you were talking there, a few years ago, I was doing quite a lot of research on schizophrenia. And I wrote a book on the near-death experience with a guy called Dr Mahendra Perera, who's an Australian psychiatrist. And he, when he was studying, he, when he did his PhD, rather than his doctor's degree, he studied on, he specialised in schizophrenia. (1:30:35)

And he worked with a guy called Alex Jenner, who was Professor of Psychiatry at Leeds University. And he put me in contact with Alex. And I had the opportunity to have a very long chat with one of the world's leading experts on schizophrenia. This guy had spent 45 years of his life researching schizophrenia and allied experiences, you know, like TLA and everything else. (1:31:00)

And I asked him, and I said, so you're one of the world's leading experts on schizophrenia. What is it? And he said, I've absolutely no idea. He said, all I know is it is not one typology. There are so many different facets of this. We've lumped it together because we have no idea what it is. And I would argue that within my Huxleyan spectrum, I would argue that the same can be said for the schizophore epilepsy, isn't there, on the extremes of epilepsy, there's the schizophore elements. (1:31:28)

And I know that my friend Myron Dial overlaps into that area. And as he said, you know, and Myron has been on this show a couple of times, you know, that the doors of perception are so open for these individuals that they can't even function correctly because there's so much information coming in. The filters just aren't working anymore. (1:31:51)

The filters have gone. They've blown off. So no wonder they act erratically. It's because they can't deal with it. And I think, you know, that we could pull into here, as I say, autism and various other things, because I think a lot of these areas, they have elements of each other in one way or another. (1:32:10)

And we need to think, well, you know, where's the feedback mechanisms taking place here? What can this tell us? Instead of compartmentalising them, let's re-look at them again and let's talk to the people who experience them. That's what you should be doing. That's what that's what you're doing. And that's why your work is so important. (1:32:32)

You know, absolutely. Right. I'm aware of getting towards the end now. So, Louise, can you let us know how anybody that's fascinated by this can contact you, check out your website, everything else? So where can they come to? (1:32:42)

So I can be contacted on louise.spires at northampton.ac.uk, my university address, and the university also holds details of my research. So if somebody looks up Louise Spires Northampton University, then they will see they will see the details. That's no problem. I guess that you hold details on your website. Yeah, I will. I will put up the links as well. (1:33:27)

Yeah, because the the the link for the for the research, which I can put in the chat room, is quite long. So so whilst I can read it out for people, whilst they're desperately scribbling it down, I'll put it in the chat. Well, no, because it's sort of been recorded anyway. That's probably the best way or contact me. (1:33:49)

Yeah. And it's also if you're if you're really desperate and you can't remember my name and how to get there, then Epilepsy Action, who I'm working with, they've been very supportive, actually. And they've got the survey advertised on their research page as well. So you can always go in through Epilepsy Action's research page and they have it advertised to. Wonderful. So that's the way to do it. (1:34:12)

Wonderful, because funnily enough, Myron's just made a comment from America. No doctor has ever explained my experiences. I just have them. Sorry about that. And it's true, isn't it? You know, it's the trying to compartmentalize the extraordinary. Yeah. And that's not. It's not my desire. My desire is to say, aren't we aren't we wonderful? Don't we all have access to something amazing? And and shouldn't that be honored? Absolutely. Is there anything that we've missed that you think from our conversation that you'd like to mention now or anything or, you know, do you feel? Oh, goodness me, no. (1:34:50)

I think we've spoken about so much and I could talk forever about this stuff. I don't know about you, but it's so it's it's and and the crossover, I think, with different conditions. People are always asking me, I have schizophrenia. Do you think it's like this? I think, you know, people who are non neurotypical have a different way of engaging. Sarah, have you got any final points? I also think neurotypical is a bit of a misnomer, really, because everyone's like an individual fingerprint and we're bound to be the same neurologically as we are fingerprint wise as well. (1:35:33)

So I don't think this idea of being neurotypical holds that much water. And actually, you know, we've said it before so many times on this show in terms of especially neuroscience, the materialist reductionist view of neuroscience as being that the character of a person, the emotional state of a person, the psychology of a person can be determined by just looking at that brain is not even scientific anyway. (1:35:56)

And so if we're getting to a point in science where we're recognising the interconnectedness of species, let's say through mycelial networks, then I think we're going to start to understand that human beings have a similar, perhaps not yet visible or well understood mycelial network themselves and that we're all interconnected. (1:36:15)

And that's actually a much more scientific way to look at life on this planet. And this also means that we can, like you say, honour those kinds of experiences as being perhaps sometimes overwhelming, uncomfortable and unpleasant experiences of too much information coming in simultaneously where someone can't function. And therefore, you know, I have friends that have a lot of issues whereby they experience really scary psychotic breaks and this kind of stuff. And I don't think you want to downplay that in terms of and also the same sort of delusions of grandeur and Jesus complex and this kind of stuff. (1:36:51)

Like, I think everything needs to be looked at on an individual basis, bearing in mind that we're all connected at the same time, so that the understanding that we're part of this interconnected cosmos can inform and educate the experience of an individual and that the reality of us all being interconnected is modulated through an individual's understanding and perception of the world. (1:37:17)

So it's fed by the culture of that person as they grow up and that changes the way they view these anomalous experiences, I think, quite often. But I do think, you know, it's interesting that you brought up Zikiku because I study ancient dreaming cultures and Zikiku means ghost or spirit in Sumerian and it relates to a book of dream omens, a series of dream omens, the Ishkar Zikiku. And in Babylonia, you wouldn't just have a physical physician doctor, you'd also have an Ashiku, a spirit doctor. (1:37:51)

So there's always been an awareness of spirit and if we were to return to a culture where we acknowledged that human beings even have a spirit and that we're part of a divine conscious cosmos, then we wouldn't have these problems in the first place. Culture is sick and the world is sick and society is sick and I think we'd probably find there'd be a lot less sick individuals if our culture and our society wasn't so sick. (1:38:19)

Well said. Well said, Sarah. Very impressive. That's good. Right, okay, very much. Thanks everybody for listening in. As usual, this has been recorded and it will go up as a recording tomorrow and then it will be up there for permanent viewing. So if anybody wants to watch this again, and I'm sure many people will, you have the opportunity there. Also, if you can share it with as many people as you possibly can, because this is Louise's work is incredibly important, as we've tried to stress, and it's important that we get this out there as well. Just let everybody know that at the moment our next guest will be on the 13th of August and we've got Rizwan Virk joining us from California, which means that we'll be going out slightly later. (1:39:02)

So we'll probably go out around about eight o'clock UK time and he'll be joining us from there. And this is going to be a fascinating discussion on the latest research in terms of the true nature of reality and everything else as well. So if you can join us for that, that would be really wonderful. (1:39:18)

So everybody, thanks very much again and we'll speak to you soon. Okay, thanks very much and goodbye again. And my thanks again to Sarah and thanks again to Louise for a wonderful discussion. Bye. (1:39:26)

(2024-12-05)

entry.title: 「途中で途切れた Bigfoot の足跡」の謎を解く （途中1）
entry.content:
前置き​

Ryan Burns は Skinwalker ranch の南側に隣接した土地を購入して所有しており、"Space Wolf Reserch" と名付けている。

その所有地で起きた「途中で途切れた Bigfoot の足跡」の事件を取り上げ、その謎を解く(*1)。

これまでも「途中で途切れた Bigfoot の足跡」について多数の報告があり、証拠の 写真/動画 のデータも提示されてきた。それらのデータから「Bigfoot が portal（異次元空間ゲート） の類を通って 別次元/別空間 へ移動したのだ」…的な解釈が横行している。

だが、今回の動画で提示されている状況証拠から全く別の合理的な機序があることに気付いた。この動画撮影者を含め、誰一人としてこの機序に気づいていない筈（DoD や情報機関の一部は気づいているかも）。

なお、ここでは

敷地に設置した 4トンのコンテナが勝手に移動した ⇒ この謎を解く

という事件も起きている。

(*1)​

途中で途切れる Bigfoot の足跡の謎とその解明については、

Missing-411 や Bigfoot : 足跡が途中で途絶える現象 → 合理的に説明する （途中2） (2023-02-23)
